title: Dota2 Senate
description:
# Dota2 Senate

Two parties, Radiant and Dire, are voting in a circular senate. The input string `senate` gives the initial order of senators:

* `R` means a Radiant senator.
* `D` means a Dire senator.

Voting proceeds from left to right. After the last senator in the current order, the next active senator is again the earliest surviving senator, so the process repeats in rounds.

When an active senator gets a turn, they must choose one action:

1. **Ban one opponent.** The chosen opponent loses the right to act in the current and all later rounds.
2. **Announce victory.** This is allowed only when every senator who still has voting rights belongs to the same party.

Every senator plays optimally for their own party. Return `"Radiant"` if Radiant can force the final announcement, otherwise return `"Dire"`.

## Key Clarification

Senators who remain active act again in the next round, keeping their original relative order.

## Example 1:

**Input:** senate = "RD"
**Output:** "Radiant"
**Explanation:** The first Radiant senator acts before the Dire senator, bans that Dire senator, and is the only active senator in the next round.

## Example 2:

**Input:** senate = "RDD"
**Output:** "Dire"
**Explanation:** The first Radiant senator bans the next Dire senator. The remaining Dire senator still gets a turn in this round, bans the Radiant senator, and later announces victory.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= senate.length <= 10^4`
* `senate[i]` is either `R` or `D`.

solutions.name: Two Queues Greedy
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store the original indices of Radiant senators in one queue and Dire senators in another queue. The smaller front index acts first, bans the other front senator, and comes back in the next round by being reinserted with index `current + n`.

## Key Insight

Comparing the two front indices is enough to know who acts first among the next Radiant and Dire senators. Reinserting the winner with `+ n` preserves the circular order without simulating every empty slot.

## Complexity Analysis

Each senator is removed at most once by a ban, so the total number of queue operations is linear.

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Single Queue Pending Bans
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep one queue of active senators in turn order. When a senator survives their current turn, they add one pending ban against the opposite party and go to the back of the queue for a future round. When a senator is consumed by a pending ban, their party count decreases and they are not reinserted.

## Key Insight

A pending ban does not need to remember the exact target. Because everyone wants their party to win, the best use of a ban is always to remove the next active opponent before that opponent can act.

## Complexity Analysis

Every queue poll either removes one senator permanently or lets one senator issue a ban that will remove an opponent later, so the process performs a linear number of effective events.

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Boolean Array Round Simulation
solutions.description:
## Approach

Simulate the senate order directly. A boolean array marks senators whose rights have already been removed. Pending bans are counted for both parties and are applied to the next active opponent encountered in later positions or later rounds.

## Key Insight

This route mirrors the statement most closely: skipped senators stay skipped, and unused bans carry forward across the end of a round. It is slower than the queue greedy approach but useful for checking the process definition.

## Complexity Analysis

In the worst case the scan may repeat many rounds before one party disappears.

- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Round Buffer Simulation
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build the next round as a new string. A senator who is banned is not copied to the next round. A senator who survives adds a pending ban against the opposite party and is copied forward.

## Key Insight

The important detail is that pending bans can cross a round boundary. If a ban is created near the end of one scan, it may remove an opponent at the beginning of the next scan.

## Complexity Analysis

Repeatedly rebuilding the surviving order is direct and readable, but it can require many scans in adversarial orders.

- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n)
